stories.title: Qube Inks 52K-SF Deal at Related and Oxford’s 70 Hudson Yards Development
stories.excerpt: Related Companies and Oxford Properties’ 70 Hudson Yards — a roughly 1.4 million-square-foot office tower that won’t be complete until 2028 — has secured another office tenant, Commercial Observer has learned. Qube, a global investment manager, has agreed to lease 52,000 square feet at the planned 52-story office building currently under development in Manhattan’s Hudson Yards, according to a source with knowledge of the deal and confirmed by Avison Young’s third-quarter Manhattan office report. The length of the lease and the asking rent were unclear, but Avison Young’s report found office asking rents in Hudson Yards averaged $117.66 per square foot during the third quarter of 2026. It’s also unclear who brokered the deal. Spokespeople for Related, Oxford, Avison Young and Qube did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Qube currently has a New York City office listed across the street at 50 Hudson Yards and will likely relocate once the new 70 Hudson Yards tower is complete. News of the Qube deal comes after financial advisory firm Deloitte signed a lease in April 2025 to anchor 70 Hudson Yards with 800,000 square feet, as CO previously reported. That deal was signed long before the planned tower between West 35th and West 36th streets broke ground in June 2025. Deloitte will consolidate its current offices — including its current HQ at 30 Rockefeller Plaza — into its new space at 70 Hudson Yards. Once complete, the new tower will feature event spaces, private dining areas, a podcast studio and an 8,000-square-foot terrace. Related and Oxford’s megaproject in Hudson Yards, designed by Roger Ferris + Partners and Gensler, is planned as New York City’s first zero-carbon-emission skyscraper and represents one of the largest ground-up office developments in the U.S. since the COVID pandemic. It joins a roster of ambitious office developments going up in Manhattan. In October, J.P. Morgan Chase opened its new headquarters building at 270 Park Avenue. The $4
bullets: Qube leases 52K SF at Related/Oxford's 70 Hudson Yards, Manhattan office tower completing 2028
Hudson Yards office asking rents averaged $117.66/SF in Q3 2026; tower still pre-completion
Tenant commitment signals pre-completion leasing momentum in competitive Hudson Yards submarket
stories.summary: Qube, a global investment manager, has leased 52,000 square feet at 70 Hudson Yards, a 1.4 million-square-foot, 52-story office tower under development by Related and Oxford Properties and scheduled to complete in 2028. The deal occurs in a market where Hudson Yards office asking rents averaged $117.66 per square foot in Q3 2026. Qube currently occupies space at 50 Hudson Yards and will relocate to the new tower.
stories.impact: Pre-completion office leasing at trophy developments indicates sustained Manhattan CBD demand from institutional tenants, though the 2028 delivery extends the supply timeline. For multifamily developers: office strength and corporate footprint growth in Hudson Yards and Midtown West signal sustained white-collar job density—favorable long-term demand fundamentals for rental housing in adjacent neighborhoods (Hell's Kitchen, Clinton), but no immediate supply pressure that would force rent compression in nearby multifamily assets.

stories.title: Alcion Ventures, Slate Offload 60 East 12th Street for $83M
stories.excerpt: A joint venture of Alcion Ventures and Slate Property Group is parting ways with a rental apartment building near Manhattan’s Union Square at a loss, Commercial Observer has learned. The JV, using the entity 60 East 12th Street Owner, has sold the 133-unit 60 East 12th Street to Stonehenge Investment and Wraith Capital Group for $82.5 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The sale price is a roughly 23.3 percent discount from the $107.5 million Alcion and Slate bought the property for in an off-market deal from Heller Realty in 2019. Alcion has a 91 percent stake in the site, while Slate holds a 9 percent stake. Built in 1962, the 13-story 60 East 12th Street has a mix of apartments ranging from studios to three-bedrooms and includes 5,100 square feet of ground-level retail space, all of which seems to be currently occupied by an attached Metropolis parking garage. No brokers were involved in the new sale, according to the source. It’s unclear what Stonehenge and Wraith Capital are planning for the property between Broadway and Fourth Avenue, but the building will likely remain residential, as Stonehenge manages and invests in multifamily assets in New York City. Spokespeople for Alcion, Slate, Stonehenge and Wraith Capital did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The sale comes as Alcion winds down its operations and liquidates its assets, the source said. The Boston-based real estate private equity firm was founded in 2005 and focuses on value-add and opportunistic investments across the U.S. Alcion has been on a selling streak of its properties in recent years, including several residential and mixed-use properties in Brooklyn. Last year, Alcion and Golub & Company also listed One East Delaware, a 37-story apartment tower in Chicago, on the market after purchasing it for $146 million in 2016, The Real Deal reported. bullets: Alcion Ventures/Slate sell 133-unit Union Square rental building for $82.5M, 23% below 2019 cost
Property purchased for $107.5M in 2019, offloaded at substantial loss to Stonehenge Investment/Wraith Capital
Manhattan residential market showing forced liquidation at discount despite tight supply narrative
stories.summary: Alcion Ventures and Slate Property Group have sold 60 East 12th Street, a 133-unit rental apartment building near Union Square in Manhattan, to Stonehenge Investment and Wraith Capital Group for $82.5 million—a 23.3 percent discount from the $107.5 million they paid Heller Realty for it in an off-market deal in 2019. The 13-story building, built in 1962, contains studios through three-bedroom units and 5,100 square feet of ground-level retail space currently leased to a Metropolis parking garage. No brokers facilitated the transaction.
stories.impact: A forced sale at 23% loss suggests underlying capital cost pressures or underperformance at this core Manhattan rental asset despite supposedly tight supply. This signals that recent rent growth and market rhetoric may not have fully offset higher financing costs (debt service jumped post-2022 rate hikes) or that these sponsors overpaid in 2019. For multifamily developers: similar vintage core Manhattan rentals underwritten at pre-2022 cost-of-capital assumptions may face margin compression or refinancing risk, requiring higher rent growth assumptions or conservative equity returns to justify new development at current costs in prime Manhattan submarkets.

stories.title: Plymouth Waterfront Hotel Set for Renovations
stories.excerpt: Haynes, a Massachusetts- and Rhode Island-based construction management firm, is leading a multi-level renovation of Hotel 1620, a boutique waterfront hotel in historic Plymouth, MA operated by Linchris and included in its Independent Collection of Hotels. Slated to begin in early November, the renovation encompasses a new main lobby and reception area, along with an adjoining work lounge, micro market, pub, pre-function corridor and new public restrooms. On the first floor, Haynes is renovating the indoor pool cabana, event room, adjacent fitness corridor and additional public restrooms. Work on the third and fourth floors extends to the elevator lobbies. Designed by Corgan, a Texas-based architectural firm, in collaboration with owner Linchris Hotel Corporation, the renovation introduces a coastal New England aesthetic that complements the hotel’s harborside setting in Plymouth, according to Haynes. bullets: Hotel 1620 in Plymouth, MA undergoing multi-level renovation led by Haynes construction; work starts November
Renovation includes lobby, restaurant, pool cabana, fitness, event spaces; designed by Corgan Architects

stories.summary: Haynes, a Massachusetts and Rhode Island-based construction management firm, is leading a multi-level renovation of Hotel 1620, a boutique waterfront hotel in Plymouth, Massachusetts, operated by Linchris Hotels. The renovation—slated to begin in November and designed by Corgan Architects—encompasses a new main lobby, reception area, work lounge, micro market, pub, indoor pool cabana, event room, fitness corridor, and updated elevators and restrooms across multiple floors, introducing a coastal New England aesthetic.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Hospitality renovation reflects strong leisure travel and experiential tourism demand in coastal New England markets, but does not signal job creation, population migration, or housing demand drivers. No material implication for residential rental demand or capital flows into apartment development.

stories.title: Affirmed Housing Breaks Ground on Affordable TOD in La Mesa
stories.excerpt: The San Diego Metropolitan Transit System (MTS) and Affirmed Housing held the groundbreaking of Spring View, the latest transit-oriented affordable housing community to result from the organizations’ longstanding partnership. Located at the Spring Street Transit Center in La Mesa, the nearly $116-million development will provide 145 affordable homes and two manager units with convenient access to public transportation. “Creating more accessible housing resources means thinking beyond the four walls of a home and considering how residents connect with everything they need to thrive,” said Jimmy Silverwood, president of Affirmed Housing. “Our longstanding partnership with MTS has allowed us to bring that approach to life by pairing high-quality affordable housing with convenient transit access.” The development is supported by a variety of public and private funding sources, including: HUD-VASH and HUD Project-Based Vouchers through the County of San Diego; IHTF, HOME and HOME-ARP funds, also from the County of San Diego; California Department of Housing and Community Developments’ Infill Infrastructure Grant Program; the California Tax Allocation Committee; the California Debt Limit Allocation Committee; U.S. Bank; and Citibank. The post Affirmed Housing Breaks Ground on Affordable TOD in La Mesa appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Affirmed Housing breaks ground on Spring View: 145-unit affordable TOD in La Mesa, San Diego; $116M total cost
Located at Spring Street Transit Center; mix of HUD vouchers, state grants, and private financing (U.S. Bank, Citibank)
Public-private affordable housing pipeline in transit-rich submarket; heavy reliance on subsidy stack
stories.summary: Affirmed Housing and the San Diego Metropolitan Transit System held groundbreaking for Spring View, a $116 million transit-oriented affordable housing development at the Spring Street Transit Center in La Mesa. The project will deliver 145 affordable homes and two manager units with direct transit access. Financing is composed of HUD-VASH and Project-Based Vouchers, California state grants (IHTF, HOME, HOME-ARP), California Tax Allocation funds, and lender commitments from U.S. Bank and Citibank.
stories.impact: Affirmed Housing's TOD pipeline in La Mesa signals sustained public and philanthropic capital flowing into affordable/workforce housing in San Diego's transit corridors. For market-rate multifamily developers: the density of subsidized affordable units near transit (Spring Street center) may suppress nearby market-rate rents if the TOD attracts lower-income households, but also indicates strong zoning flexibility and public support for transit-adjacent housing in the submarket. The tight subsidy stack (HUD vouchers + state + bank capital) reflects constrained affordable economics; market-rate developers should monitor whether public resources crowd-out private capital or create positive spillovers (transit ridership, neighborhood investment).

stories.title: RFQ Seeks Design-Build Team to Reconstruct Coney Island Boardwalk
stories.excerpt: The New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) and the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation on Wednesday released a Request for Qualifications seeking a design-build team to lead the full reconstruction of the historic Riegelmann Boardwalk in Coney Island. The RFQ is the first formal step in delivering the more than $1 billion committed by the city to rebuild the nearly century-old boardwalk. The new structure will be built to withstand stronger storms and rising seas. “Today marks a key milestone in the city’s more than $1-billion commitment to the future of the historic boardwalk, and NYCEDC looks forward to seeing the industry’s leading minds compete for this critical project,” said NYCEDC president & CEO Anthony Shorris. The RFQ invites qualified teams to demonstrate their experience delivering large-scale, complex waterfront infrastructure. Following review, NYCEDC will issue a Request for Proposals to a shortlist of qualified teams this winter, with selection of a design-build team expected in spring 2027. Responses to the RFQ are due Nov. 4. The post RFQ Seeks Design-Build Team to Reconstruct Coney Island Boardwalk appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC Economic Development Corp. releases RFQ for Coney Island Boardwalk reconstruction; $1B+ public commitment
Riegelmann Boardwalk nearly century-old; new structure to withstand stronger storms, rising seas; selection spring 2027
Large-scale waterfront infrastructure rebuild signals climate adaptation and leisure district revitalization in Brooklyn
stories.summary: The New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) and Department of Parks and Recreation released a Request for Qualifications seeking a design-build team to lead the full reconstruction of the historic Riegelmann Boardwalk in Coney Island. The city has committed more than $1 billion to the project, which will rebuild the nearly 100-year-old boardwalk to withstand stronger storms and rising sea levels. Team selection is expected in spring 2027 following an RFP process this winter.
stories.impact: A $1B+ public commitment to Coney Island waterfront infrastructure signals NYC's intent to stabilize and invest in this leisure/tourism district as a climate-resilient destination. For multifamily developers: the boardwalk reconstruction will drive localized property investment and hospitality/retail activity, potentially unlocking residential development opportunities in adjacent Coney Island and Sheepshead Bay submarkets. However, timing (completion well beyond 2027) is long-term; near-term, heightened public scrutiny of waterfront climate resilience may increase development costs and entitlement timelines for any residential projects in the area.

stories.title: Mercedes-Benz Miami Project’s $1.1B Financing Package Speeds Closer to Completion
stories.excerpt: Ladies and gents, start your engines. Mercedes-Benz Places–Miami’s construction financing is officially off to the races, sources confirmed to Commercial Observer. J.P. Morgan is leading the $1.11 billion financing package for the luxury-branded, mixed-use tower in Miami’s Brickell neighborhood and providing a $860 million construction loan. Nuveen Green Capital is also in the process of providing roughly $250 million in Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing for the project. While term sheets have now been signed, the deal has not yet closed. It’s expected to close by year end, sources said. Walker & Dunlop’s Aaron Appel, Dustin Stolly, Jonathan Schwartz, Adam Schwartz, Keith Kurland, Sean Reimer and Sean Bastian are negotiating the financing. The Promote first reported news of the mammoth loan being in the works. JDS Development was the developer behind the Miami project, but Fontainebleau Development, led by Jeffrey Soffer, stepped in as a partner in the deal earlier this year to move the development forward after it became embroiled in a foreclosure suit. When completed, the 67-story Mercedes-Benz Places-Miami, at 140 SW 11th Street, will include 791 luxury condos, 130,000 square feet of amenities, including a cocktail bar and two restaurants and wellness facilities, 200,000 square feet of office space, a 174-key hotel, a parking garage and a park. Sources said that J.P. Morgan’s loan is collateralized by the entire Mercedes-Benz project, while Nuveen’s will be collateralized by its commercial component only. The German car manufacturer first lent its name to the Brickell tower in 2024, marking Mercedes-Benz’s first branded real estate project in the U.S. It followed the proliferation of towers by competitors Porsche, Aston Martin and Bentley. bullets: Mercedes-Benz Places Miami closes $1.11B financing: J.P. Morgan $860M construction loan + $250M C-PACE from Nuveen
Luxury mixed-use tower in Brickell; expected to close by year-end; Fontainebleau Developments taking over from JDS
Large construction financing package closing signals restored capital appetite for luxury urban mixed-use in South Florida
stories.summary: Mercedes-Benz Places Miami has secured a $1.11 billion construction financing package, with J.P. Morgan leading and providing an $860 million construction loan and Nuveen Green Capital providing approximately $250 million in Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing. Term sheets have been signed and closing is expected by year-end. Fontainebleau Developments has taken over the project from JDS Development Group. The luxury-branded mixed-use tower is located in Miami's Brickell neighborhood.
stories.impact: A $1.1B construction close for a branded luxury mixed-use tower signals strong capital availability and sponsor confidence in Miami Brickell's high-end market. For multifamily developers: the deal underscores that large-scale financing for signature projects is flowing; however, the dominance of luxury/mixed-use development in Brickell (and downtown Miami more broadly) reflects capital chasing trophy assets and branded products. This may tighten financing for core multifamily or workforce housing in the same submarket. Developers should note the C-PACE financing component (Nuveen) as an alternative source of construction capital, though it requires sustainability credentials.

stories.title: Walker Webcast: Chris Lee and KKR’s Different Investment Regime
stories.excerpt: When Chris Lee appeared on the Walker Webcast in February 2023, KKR Real Estate’s Partner and President said the firm was becoming more constructive about putting capital to work. Higher yields, improving capital flows, and increasingly attractive asset pricing were creating what Lee called a favorable risk-reward environment. Three and a half years later, Lee told Walker & Dunlop Chairman and CEO Willy Walker that KKR still sees plenty of opportunities. But the framework has changed. “We think about it as a regime change,” Lee said during his Sept. 30 return to the Walker Webcast. He explained that the post-GFC environment of lower interest rates, monetary and fiscal stimulus and relatively benign globalization has given way to higher rates, inflation concerns, heavily leveraged government balance sheets, geopolitical uncertainty, and an economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence and digitization. That backdrop has changed how KKR approaches both sides of its roughly $85 billion real estate portfolio, which is divided almost evenly between credit and equity. “We’re taking a pretty balanced approach right now,” Lee said. On the credit side, “we have bank capital, we have insurance capital, fixed and floating, and then we have more opportunistic lending capital,” Lee said. “We’re very active in all of those markets, and we’re in all those asset classes. We’re also active across the U.S. and Europe.” He went on to say that more opportunities exist, especially as five-year loans are approaching maturity. KKR is comfortable with existing multifamily credit exposure because the firm has generally avoided high-leverage lending and focuses heavily on sponsors. On the equity side, however, KKR is considerably more selective than it was when Lee appeared on the 2023 webcast. “When we think about our investment strategy, we are looking for demand trends that we think are attractive long term,” Lee said. bullets: KKR Real Estate shifts to 'regime change' investment framework: higher rates, inflation, geopolitical risk, AI disruption
KKR manages ~$85B real estate portfolio (credit and equity nearly evenly split); pursuing balanced approach
Macro headwinds prompting major capital allocators to recalibrate underwriting and risk tolerance in real estate
stories.summary: Chris Lee, KKR Real Estate's Partner and President, told Walker & Dunlop CEO Willy Walker that KKR is operating under a new investment regime. The post-GFC era of low rates, stimulus, and benign globalization has shifted to higher rates, inflation, heavily leveraged government balance sheets, geopolitical uncertainty, and AI-driven economic change. KKR is taking a balanced approach across its roughly $85 billion real estate portfolio, which is divided almost evenly between credit and equity, and is seeking to deploy capital more selectively.
stories.impact: A major capital provider reframing its entire real estate investment thesis signals broad-based caution and underwriting tightness across the industry. For multifamily developers: KKR's pivot to a 'regime change' mentality—favoring higher equity returns, more selective geography/product, and shorter hold periods—will trickle down to equity commitments and cost-of-capital for mid-market and core-plus development. Developers should expect higher return hurdles (8–12%+), more conservative underwriting on rent-growth assumptions, and capital to concentrate in Tier-1 markets and strong demographic fundamentals rather than secondary-market or growth-story positions.

stories.title: Uncertain Times Demand Fresh Construction Project Management Strategies
stories.excerpt: For construction company owners, uncertainty has become a permanent part of project planning. Steel prices can shift with tariff policy and global demand, fuel costs can respond to geopolitical conflict thousands of miles from a jobsite, equipment lead times can stretch for nearly a year, and skilled labor remains constrained. At the same time, owners are being asked to deliver projects faster and with greater cost and schedule certainty. This environment is redefining project management. Owners increasingly need construction expertise, market intelligence and procurement insight during the earliest stages of a project, helping guide when critical design, sequencing and purchasing decisions can have the greatest effect on budgets and schedules. George Swetz. Photo: Skanska USA At Skanska Integrated Solutions, we support owners from early planning and preconstruction through construction and completion. Drawing on Skanska’s decades of experience delivering complex projects, our teams bring a builder’s perspective to decisions involving cost, schedule, procurement, constructability and risk. Skanska’s Summer 2026 Construction Market Trends Report illustrates the challenge. Construction demand remains strong, but is increasingly concentrated in data centers, infrastructure, power generation, advanced manufacturing, pharmaceutical production and select health care markets. For many owners, the challenge is not identifying projects to build, but securing the labor, equipment, materials and power required to deliver them. Consider materials and equipment. Structural steel lead times are reaching 40 to 50 weeks in some markets, while HVAC equipment can take as long as 52 weeks. Prices for larger generators are expected to increase 8 to 10 percent in 2026, and HVAC equipment pricing could rise 10 to 12 percent. bullets: Construction owners facing persistent uncertainty: steel tariffs, fuel prices, equipment lead-times (up to 1 year), labor constraints
Industry shifting toward early-stage preconstruction and procurement expertise to lock costs and manage risk
Project management strategies evolving to address cost inflation and schedule uncertainty across the development pipeline
stories.summary: Construction companies and owners are navigating a new environment of permanent uncertainty: steel prices fluctuate with tariff policy, fuel costs respond to geopolitical events, equipment lead times stretch to nearly a year, and skilled labor remains constrained. Simultaneously, owners are being asked to deliver projects faster with greater cost and schedule certainty. Firms like Skanska are responding by embedding builder expertise and market intelligence in early planning and preconstruction phases to influence design, sequencing, and procurement decisions when they have the greatest budget and schedule impact.
stories.impact: The emphasis on early-stage preconstruction and procurement risk management directly affects multifamily development feasibility and timelines. For developers: locking material costs (steel, lumber, mechanical equipment) and labor 18–24 months before construction start has become critical to avoid post-award cost overruns. This lengthens the pre-construction phase, delays groundbreaking, and increases soft costs. Developers should budget 10–15% contingency premiums for tariff/commodity volatility and plan 12–18 month equipment lead-times into critical-path scheduling. Projects with fixed-price general contracts and locked-in material costs will be more competitive; cost-plus models carry unacceptable downside risk.

stories.title: JLL IPT pays $90M for Worcester Industrial
stories.excerpt: JLL Income Property Trust (JLL IPT) has acquired Worcester Distribution Center, a Class A industrial building in the Western Boston submarket, for a purchase price of approximately $90 million. The seller was not disclosed. Built in 2022, the property totals approximately 396,000 square feet and is 100% leased to a single tenant on a long-term lease. “Worcester Distribution Center is an important addition to our expanding industrial portfolio,” said Allan Swaringen, JLL IPT president and CEO. “The cost of fuel has continued to rise, widening the imbalance between the costs of transportation and rent. As a result, demand for well-located industrial properties proximate to nodes of critical transportation infrastructure has increased. We have long prioritized logistics centers near these key transportation epicenters, and Worcester Distribution Center aligns with our industrial strategy to position a meaningful share of the portfolio to capitalize on these longer-term demand drivers.” The post JLL IPT pays $90M for Worcester Industrial appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JLL Income Property Trust acquires Worcester Distribution Center for ~$90M; 396K SF Class A industrial, 100% leased
Purpose-built 2022 facility; single long-term tenant; located in Western Boston near critical transportation infrastructure
Institutional industrial capital targeting logistics nodes; fuel cost pressures widening arbitrage between transportation and rent
stories.summary: JLL Income Property Trust (JLL IPT) has acquired Worcester Distribution Center, a Class A industrial building in Western Boston, for approximately $90 million. Built in 2022 and totaling approximately 396,000 square feet, the property is 100 percent leased to a single tenant on a long-term lease. JLL IPT cited rising fuel costs as widening the imbalance between transportation and logistics rent, making well-located industrial properties near key transportation nodes increasingly attractive.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Institutional capital's focus on last-mile logistics in secondary industrial nodes (Worcester vs. Boston proper) reflects post-pandemic e-commerce density shifts and fuel-arbitrage economics. For multifamily developers: if e-commerce logistics and industrial jobs are concentrating in Worcester and similar secondary industrial corridors, rental demand may shift toward those submarkets (Worcester, Framingham, Providence) rather than close-in urban cores. However, Worcester's industrial uptake does not signal residential amenity or population inflows; monitor whether logistics employment translates to residential workforce housing demand or simply relocates lower-wage jobs to lower-cost areas with minimal rental uplift.

stories.title: Billionaire Josh Harris’s Firm Moving to New Miami Design District Dev
stories.excerpt: Developer Craig Robins has signed up office tenants at the newest development within the Miami Design District luxury mall, including the private equity firm of billionaire Josh Harris, who co-founded financial behemoth Apollo Global Management and owns the Washington Commanders NFL team. In the biggest transaction, Atria Health Research signed a 55,000-square-foot lease at the Sweetbird North mixed-use development. The company, which offers medical concierge services, charges a $60,000 annual membership fee after a one-time $100,000 initiation fee. It will occupy the third, fourth, and fifth floors of the eight-story development. Sweetbird North broke ground Wednesday after securing a $125 million construction loan from French bank Crédit Agricole last month. Construction is expected to be complete in 2028. The 120,000-square-foot development, which includes 92,000 square feet of office space and 22,500 square feet of ground-floor retail space, abuts the Museum Garage at 95 Northeast 40th Street, across the street from Alo and Alice + Olivia stores. The sponsors of the project designed by world-renowned Snøhetta include the original backers of the 18-block mall, Miami Design District Associates: Robins’s Miami-based Dracra, LVMH-backed L Catterton Real Estate and Bernard Arnault’s family office. New York-based private equity firm Raycliff Capital, another sponsor of Sweetbird North, will be taking a floor at the development. 26North Partners, the firm Harris founded in 2022 after stepping down from Apollo Global Management, will take another floor. The New York-based private equity firm was previously based at 404 Washington Avenue, an eight-story, mixed-use building in Miami Beach. Sweetbird North is part of a broader expansion at the Miami Design District, which has become a popular luxury mall home to Prada, Chanel and Hermes boutiques. bullets: Josh Harris's firm (Apollo co-founder) signs major lease at Sweetbird North, Miami Design District; $125M construction loan closed
Atria Health Research leases 55K SF (floors 3–5) of 120K SF mixed-use development; $60K annual membership concierge service
High-end Design District office attracting ultra-premium tenants; mixed-use development on track for 2028 completion
stories.summary: Developer Craig Robins has signed office tenants at Sweetbird North, a new mixed-use development in Miami's Design District luxury mall, including Josh Harris's private equity firm (Harris co-founded Apollo Global Management). Atria Health Research, a medical concierge service charging $60,000 annual memberships, has leased 55,000 square feet across floors 3–5. Sweetbird North broke ground this week after securing a $125 million construction loan from Crédit Agricole and is expected to complete in 2028. The 120,000-square-foot development includes 92,000 square feet of office and 22,500 square feet of ground-floor retail.
stories.impact: Sweetbird North's pre-opening leasing to ultra-high-net-worth tenants (private equity, luxury concierge) and $125M debt close signal strong capital availability for trophy mixed-use projects in Miami's Design District. For multifamily developers: the Design District is zoning and financing high-end mixed-use office/retail, not residential, concentrating capital and institutional leasing in this micromarket. This may suppress multifamily development density in the immediate Design District but indirectly supports nearby residential demand (Wynwood, Buena Vista, Allapattah) as affluent tenants at Sweetbird North seek premium rental housing within walking distance or short Uber rides. Monitor Design District office/retail absorption closely; successful pre-leasing may trigger follow-on mixed-use and luxury rental development in adjacent neighborhoods.
